q: How many fleets participated in Run on Less – Messy Middle, and how were they split across powertrain types?
expected: 13 fleets total: 4 diesel/renewable diesel (Albert Transport, Frito-Lay, Mesilla Valley Transportation, Schneider), 3 CNG/RNG (Kleysen Group, UPS, Wegmans), 4 battery electric (4Gen Logistics, Joyride Logistics, Nevoya, Saia), and 2 hydrogen fuel cell (Penske, Pilot).

selected.source: Run on Less - Messy Middle Blueprint
selected.why: This report details the Run on Less - Messy Middle demonstration, including the exact count of participating fleets and their powertrain split.

answer:
A total of 13 fleets participated in the Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 25]. 

These 13 fleets were split across four different powertrain solutions as follows [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 25]:

* **Diesel / Biodiesel / Renewable Diesel (4 fleets):** Albert Transport, Frito-Lay, Mesilla Valley Transportation, and Schneider [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 25].
* **Battery Electric (4 fleets):** 4Gen Logistics, Joyride Logistics, Nevoya, and Saia [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 25].
* **Natural Gas / Renewable Natural Gas (3 fleets):** Kleysen Group, UPS, and Wegmans [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 25].
* **Hydrogen Fuel Cell (2 fleets):** Penske and Pilot [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 25].

While there were 13 participating fleets, NACFE tracked a total of 14 vehicles because one of the battery electric fleets, Saia, operated two Tesla Semis during the demonstration [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 41, 52]. The run evaluated the performance of these heavy-duty Class 8 sleeper and day cab trucks in real-world, long-haul return-to-base and over-the-road duty cycles [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20].

q: How many drivers has NACFE engaged across all five Run on Less demonstrations to date, and how many interviews did NACFE conduct specifically for Messy Middle?
expected: 63 drivers across all five Run on Less demonstrations to date. For Messy Middle specifically, NACFE conducted 105 interviews across the 13 sites between June 3 and July 23, 2025 (48 of those interviews were with support-organization personnel rather than fleet staff).

selected.why: This blueprint report contains the exact figures for the total number of drivers engaged across all five Run on Less demonstrations to date and the number of interviews conducted for Messy Middle.

answer:
Across its five Run on Less demonstrations to date, the North American Council for Freight Efficiency (NACFE) has engaged with a total of 63 drivers performing their usual duties [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. For the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration specifically, the NACFE team conducted a total of 105 interviews [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 28, 49].

The 63 participating drivers across all five events have been crucial in documenting the real-world performance of evolving truck technologies, often volunteering to have their entire working shifts tracked and filmed [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. For the Messy Middle event, the participating drivers represented a diverse group of age and experience levels, ranging from 2 years to 48 years of driving experience [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. These drivers operated heavy-duty Class 8 sleeper and day cab trucks across four different powertrain solutions: diesel/renewable diesel, natural gas/renewable natural gas, battery electric, and hydrogen fuel cell [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 22]. 

The 105 interviews conducted for the Messy Middle event took place during site visits between June 3, 2025, and July 23, 2025 [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 28]. To capture a complete picture of the "messy middle" transition, NACFE did not limit its interviews to drivers and fleet managers; 48 of the 105 interviews were conducted with support stakeholders, including vehicle manufacturers, charging suppliers, utility representatives, funding groups, and infrastructure builders [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 28, 50]. These filmed conversations provided approximately 175 hours of raw video, which NACFE curated into more than 30 promotional and educational videos to share findings with the industry [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49, 64].

q: According to the NREL source cited in this report, what share of the trucking market does the long-haul segment represent, and what share of emissions does it contribute?
expected: Long-haul trucking is 9% of the trucking market but contributes 48% of the industry's emissions, per NREL's "Decarbonizing Medium- & Heavy-Duty On-Road Vehicles: Zero-Emission Vehicle Cost Analysis" (2022), as cited by NACFE.

selected.why: This report cites the NREL Decarbonizing Medium- & Heavy-Duty On-Road Vehicles report to state the exact market share and emissions contribution of the long-haul trucking segment.

answer:
According to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) report cited by NACFE, the Class 8 long-haul truck segment represents **9% of the trucking market** but contributes **48% of its emissions** [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20].

This disproportionate impact is the primary reason the North American Council for Freight Efficiency (NACFE) focused its 2025 "Run on Less – Messy Middle" demonstration on the Class 8 long-haul market, which includes both sleepers and day cabs [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. While long-haul operations represent a relatively small portion of the overall North American trucking industry, understanding and optimizing their high emissions profile is critical to achieving industry-wide decarbonization goals [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 22].

The NREL report containing these statistics (*Decarbonizing Medium- & Heavy-Duty On-Road Vehicles: Zero Emission Vehicles Cost Analysis*) was published in 2022 [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 71]. Because this primary source predates 2026 by more than three years, these figures may not fully reflect the current technology, market shares, or emissions profile of the long-haul trucking segment today.

answer:
Across all nine Messy Middle Bootcamp sessions, there was a total of **7,171 registrations** (comprising **1,191 unique registrants**) and a total of **1,943 attendees** (comprising **720 unique attendees**) logged [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45]. 

These metrics were recorded live during the webinars, which ran from February 11, 2025, through July 1, 2025 [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45]. Registration numbers for individual sessions ranged from a low of 619 to a high of 906, while actual live attendance for individual sessions ranged from a low of 143 to a high of 300 [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45]. These totals do not account for subsequent views of the session recordings posted on the NACFE website and YouTube [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45, 46].

q: Which of the nine Messy Middle Bootcamp sessions had the lowest total attendance, and how many people attended it?
expected: Session 7, "The Production Process of Hydrogen Fuel" (6/3/25), had the lowest total attendance at 143 (26 unique).

selected.why: This blueprint report for the Run on Less - Messy Middle demonstration includes the complete session-by-session registration and attendance table for all nine sessions of the Messy Middle Bootcamp series.

answer:
Session 7, titled "The Production Processes of Hydrogen Fuel," had the lowest total attendance of all nine Messy Middle Bootcamp sessions, drawing a total of 143 attendees when it was held on June 3, 2025 [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45]. 

For further context, this session also recorded the lowest unique attendance of the series, with only 26 unique attendees [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45]. In general, the sessions comprising the Hydrogen Unit saw the lowest live participation of the bootcamp; Session 8 ("Moving Hydrogen from Here to There") drew 166 total attendees, and Session 9 ("The Opportunities and Challenges of Selling Hydrogen") drew 159 total attendees [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45]. 

By comparison, the most popular session by total attendance was Session 4, "The Current State of HD BEV: Technologies and Capabilities," which had 300 total attendees on April 8, 2025 [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45]. NACFE notes that these figures only represent live participation, as views of the session recordings—which were later posted to the NACFE website and YouTube for continued industry education—were not tracked in these tables [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 45, 46].

q: What does this report conclude about the total cost of ownership (TCO) comparison across the four Messy Middle powertrains?
expected: Nothing yet — this report explicitly defers TCO analysis to a separate "TCO Ramifications Report" NACFE plans to publish later in 2026; no TCO comparison is presented in this document.

selected.why: This report specifically provides the comprehensive Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) analysis and cost comparisons across the four Messy Middle powertrains and five duty cycles for 2025, 2028, and 2035.

answer:
The report concludes that there is no universal date or timeline for Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) parity; instead, parity is a bespoke, operational window defined by a fleet's specific geography, duty cycle, and asset utilization [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 18, 101]. However, modeling shows that battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) are the definitive long-term economic winners by 2035, while legacy diesel’s financial advantage is finite and eroding [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 18, 101]. 

Assuming a conservative scenario with zero upfront vehicle-level incentives, BEVs are projected to achieve the lowest net TCO across all five modeled duty cycles by 2035, driven by a projected 45% drop in vehicle purchase prices and superior energy efficiency [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 101]. For example, in a regional linehaul duty cycle—measured under baseline conditions of 129,087 annual miles and a five-year payback window—the BEV TCO is projected to drop from $1.37 per mile in 2025 to $0.94 per mile in 2035 [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 30, 63, 108]. Conversely, diesel is subject to a "cost escalator" driven by emissions compliance, rising maintenance, and insurance costs [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 81, 101]. Under the same regional linehaul conditions, diesel’s TCO is projected to rise from $0.85 per mile in 2025 to $1.00 per mile in 2035 [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 108].

Meanwhile, the other two alternative powertrains serve more specialized roles:
* **CNG/RNG** offers a stable, near-term hedge (especially in 2025 and 2028) by avoiding diesel’s steep maintenance and insurance escalators without requiring massive infrastructure grid upgrades [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 21, 81]. However, because its vehicle and operational costs remain relatively flat, it is eventually overtaken by the aggressive cost-reduction curve of BEVs by 2035 in most duty cycles [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 81].
* **Hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs)** are projected to remain the most expensive option across almost all duty cycles through 2035 due to high vehicle capital costs and stubbornly expensive fuel [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 21, 81]. Their niche remains limited to high-mileage, heavy-haul over-the-road (OTR) routes where rapid fueling times and maximum payload capacities are non-negotiable [Forecasting the TCO of Powertrain Alternatives: The Messy Middle Cost Report, p. 81, 101].

q: What has NACFE found about total cost of ownership for last-mile electric delivery vans?
expected: Out of scope for this report — it covers Class 8 long-haul sleeper and day-cab trucks in Run on Less – Messy Middle only. Van and step-van findings belong to other NACFE work (e.g., the 2021 Run on Less – Electric event), which this report does not cover.

selected.why: Tracks Class 3-5 electric vans and step vans (such as Ford E-Transit and GM BrightDrop) across depot operations.
Provides detailed TCO projections across duty cycles including Urban/Metro Pickup & Delivery for battery-electric vehicles.

answer:
NACFE has found that last-mile electric delivery vans and step vans have upfront purchase costs that are much closer to parity with gas and diesel vehicles compared to heavier commercial vehicle classes, resulting in a low total cost of ownership (TCO) [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving, p. 79]. Because these vehicles typically operate on short urban routes with long overnight dwell times (often 8 to 14 hours), they can be charged slowly overnight at private depots. This allows fleets to utilize slower-speed, lower-power chargers with managed charging systems, bypassing expensive public fast-charging markups and minimizing utility demand charges [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving, p. 60, 67-68, 79]. 

In real-world tracking, NACFE analyzed last-mile delivery vans under varying daily duty cycles. At Frito-Lay’s Queens, NY depot, NACFE tracked Ford E-Transit vans equipped with a 68-kWh battery and an estimated range of 108 miles, which operated in dense urban areas with multiple stops and diminishing cargo loads [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving, p. 34]. At Purolator’s Richmond, BC depot, Motiv EPIC step vans equipped with a 127-kWh battery and an estimated range of 105 miles successfully completed daily routes of 4 to 60 miles [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving, p. 43]. These lighter fleet operations qualify as "small energy depots" because they require less than 10 MWh of power per day, translating to substantially lower costs and shorter timelines to energize the facility compared to large-scale heavy-duty depots [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving, p. 78-79].

However, NACFE notes that capturing a precise, standardized TCO for electric vans remains a challenge because standard financial spreadsheets often omit critical variables. Traditional calculations frequently overlook the positive impact of high vehicle uptime, the initial administrative learning curves of transitioning a fleet, and the value of regional operating incentives—such as California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) credits—which can drastically lower net operating costs [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving, p. 77]. To help fleets model these specific inputs, NACFE has published detailed guidance on medium-duty electric truck cost of ownership [Electric Truck Depots Are Evolving, p. 21]. While the 2024 depot study extensively details last-mile delivery vans, NACFE's subsequent 2026 TCO report narrows its scope to analyze Class 8 heavy-duty vehicles exclusively [Forecasting the TCO, p. 19, 23].

q: How many Run on Less demonstrations has NACFE conducted to date?
expected: Five, as of the Run on Less – Messy Middle report (published January 2026): 2017 (diesel long-haul), 2019 Regional, 2021 Electric, 2023 Electric DEPOT, and 2025 Messy Middle. A naive answer sourced from the older Run on Less – Electric DEPOT report (published May 2024) would say four, since it predates the Messy Middle Run and states 'NACFE has conducted four Run on Less demonstrations so far.' The current, correct count is five.

selected.why: This report explicitly states that 'Run on Less - Messy Middle' is NACFE's fifth Run on Less demonstration.

answer:
As of the publication of its January 2026 report, the North American Council for Freight Efficiency (NACFE) has conducted **five** Run on Less demonstrations [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20]. These biennial events are designed to showcase commercially available efficiency technologies operating under real-world fleet conditions [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 21]. 

The first four demonstrations in the series focused on progressive steps in diesel efficiency and battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption:
* **2017 Run on Less:** Highlighted Class 8 diesel tractors in real-world long-haul fleet operations. Over a three-week monitoring period, seven participating fleets achieved an average fuel economy of 10.1 MPG [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 62]. 
* **2019 Run on Less Regional:** Spotlighted regional haul duty cycles with 10 participating fleets. The trucks—nine powered by diesel and one by compressed natural gas (CNG)—averaged a fuel economy of either 8.3 MPG or 8.4 MPG, depending on the section of the NACFE report [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 62].
* **2021 Run on Less – Electric:** Tracked 13 fleets to demonstrate the viability of BEVs, utilizing terminal tractors, vans, step vans, medium-duty box trucks, and heavy-duty regional haul tractors [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20].
* **2023 Run on Less – Electric DEPOT:** Focused on the challenges and infrastructure of scaling electric trucks, observing 10 depots that each operated 15 or more BEVs [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20].

The fifth and most recent demonstration, the **2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle**, focused on Class 8 sleepers and day cabs operating in long-haul return-to-base and over-the-road duty cycles [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 22]. Over an 18-day period in the fall of 2025, NACFE tracked 13 fleets using four distinct powertrain options: diesel/renewable diesel, natural gas/renewable natural gas, battery electric, and hydrogen fuel cells [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 20, 66].

The current, correct total is 63.

answer:
Across its five Run on Less demonstrations, the North American Council for Freight Efficiency (NACFE) has engaged with a total of **63 drivers** performing their usual delivery duties [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. 

These drivers play a crucial role in documenting the real-world performance of new and evolving truck technologies. During the demonstrations, they volunteer to have every minute of their working shifts tracked over a three-week period, in addition to participating in interviews, photography sessions, and filming [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. Many of these participants have gone on to become industry influencers, speaking on panels and sharing their experiences with trade media [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49].

In the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle event, NACFE tracked a highly diverse group of drivers with varying backgrounds and experience levels across 13 fleets [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49]. This group ranged from seasoned veterans—such as Dave Cerretto of Wegmans with 48 years of experience and Henry Albert of Albert Transport with 43 years—to newer professionals like Latavia Walker Pickett of Schneider, who had been driving for 2 years [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 49].

q: What is the longest range demonstrated by a battery-electric Class 8 truck in NACFE's Run on Less research?
expected: The longest-range BEV NACFE has actually tracked is a PepsiCo Tesla Semi during the 2023 Run on Less – Electric DEPOT (report published May 2024): 'Tesla Semis saw ranges of 410 miles on a single charge and completed 1,076 miles in a 24-hour period' (p.39-40). The Run on Less – Messy Middle report (published January 2026) shows the 400+ mile BEV class has since become normal-fleet-operation reality rather than a single flagship vehicle, citing Joyride Logistics' Windrose sleeper tractor (705-kWh LFP pack) at up to 420 miles — while most other OEMs' production BEVs still run 150-250 miles per charge. A naive answer drawing only on the 2024 report's non-Tesla depot fleets (e.g. the OK Produce/Penske Freightliner eCascadia at 475-kWh/230 miles) would understate the 2023/2024 baseline by missing the PepsiCo Tesla Semi figure entirely.
expected_loc: p.39 (current: Windrose, ‘420 miles’); run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p.39-40 (PepsiCo Tesla Semi, ‘410 miles’ / ‘1,076 miles in 24 hours’); p.36/p.38 (eCascadia, ‘230 miles’, a lower non-Tesla baseline in the same report)

selected.why: This Run on Less report tracked battery-electric trucks across depots, including PepsiCo's Sacramento depot operating Tesla Semis and documenting their range.
This Run on Less blueprint report covers Class 8 battery-electric tractors (such as Joyride Logistics' Windrose sleeper tractor) and their demonstrated range in long-haul duty cycles.

answer:
The longest range demonstrated by a battery-electric Class 8 truck in NACFE's research is **441 miles on a single charge** [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 80]. Additionally, a battery-electric Class 8 truck demonstrated a total driving distance of **1,076 miles within a 24-hour period** by utilizing multiple fast-charging sessions [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 28, 40, 80]. Both of these milestones were achieved by Class 8 Tesla Semis operated by PepsiCo at their bottling production and distribution facility in Sacramento, California, during the 2023 *Run on Less – Electric DEPOT* demonstration [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 15, 39, 40]. 

The operating conditions for these demonstrations involved transporting heavy beverage loads of up to 82,000 lbs. [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 39]. To achieve the 1,076-mile distance in a 24-hour window, the fleet utilized "slip-seating" (where a single truck is run almost continuously by being shared by two drivers across separate shifts) [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 39]. The truck's state of charge (SOC) was maintained using Tesla’s 750 kW fast-chargers, which enabled ultra-fast turnaround times, recovering from a 10% to 95% charge in less than 30 minutes [run-on-less-electric-depot-2024, p. 40].

In the subsequent 2025 *Run on Less – Messy Middle* demonstration (published in January 2026), NACFE tracked other long-haul, battery-electric Class 8 trucks with high range capabilities [run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p. 20]. These included a Windrose battery-electric sleeper tractor operated by Joyride Logistics with a claimed range of up to 420 miles [run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p. 39], and Saia LTL Freight’s Tesla Semis, which feature a claimed 500-mile range under typical less-than-truckload (LTL) conditions [run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p. 41]. However, the 2025 report does not specify a longer *demonstrated* single-charge distance than the 441-mile benchmark recorded during the 2023 event.

q: In 2023, NACFE described typical production battery-electric truck range as 150-250 miles per charge (with Tesla's unverified 500-mile demo as an outlier achieved under near-ideal conditions and a low, 55-mph speed limit). How does that compare with what NACFE actually measured in real fleet operation during the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle?
expected: The 2023 white paper 'The Messy Middle: A Time for Action' reported that production BEVs from Daimler, Volvo, Kenworth, Peterbilt and others offered single-charge ranges of 150-250 miles, cautioning that Tesla's December 2022 500-mile demonstration used nearly 100% of battery state of charge (versus the recommended 20-80% range) and was run at California's 55 mph truck speed limit — not representative of typical operations. In the actual 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle, run in real revenue service (not a controlled demo), NACFE tracked a Windrose battery-electric sleeper (Joyride Logistics) with a real-world quoted range of up to 420 miles, and its Initial Findings list '400+ mile battery electric vehicles' among recent powertrain advancements — roughly double the typical 2023 production range, achieved in normal fleet duty cycles rather than a one-off demonstration.
expected_loc: p.26/p.30-31 (2023 baseline); current: run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p.39, p.66-67

selected.why: Provides the 2023 baseline figures on production BEV range (150-250 miles) and the Tesla 500-mile demo context.
Provides the 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle findings and vehicle specs, including real-world BEV range achievements like Joyride Logistics' 420-mile sleeper tractor.
Provides deep operational and telematics data for the 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle battery-electric deployments across fleets.

answer:
In the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle, NACFE measured real-world operations that both validated the 2023 regional range expectations and demonstrated a significant expansion in battery-electric vehicle (BEV) long-haul capabilities. For typical regional BEV platforms, the 2023 estimated single-charge range of 150 to 250 miles was confirmed to be accurate under routine working conditions [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 30]. In the 2025 Run, Nevoya's Freightliner eCascadia—utilizing a 438 kWh usable battery capacity to haul regional freight with typical payloads of 60,000 to 70,000 lbs across California's flat-to-rolling Central Valley—recorded a Probable Maximum Range (PMR) of 150 to 200 miles with a real-world efficiency of 0.60 mi/kWh [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 178, 180, 181]. Similarly, 4Gen's Volvo VNR day cab—with a 565 kWh battery six-pack operating in Southern California's Inland Empire drayage corridors on terrain with up to 3% grades—achieved a single-charge PMR of 180 to 220 miles with an efficiency of 0.54 mi/kWh [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 161, 166].

For larger-battery configurations, the 2025 Run proved that single-charge ranges have advanced significantly beyond the typical 150- to 250-mile band, proving the feasibility of longer operations. Saia’s linehaul Tesla Semi (Saia 2), running a terminal-to-terminal linehaul route in Northern California with single 53-ft trailers and an estimated 800 to 900 kWh battery pack, demonstrated a single-charge PMR of 350 to 450 miles with an efficiency of 0.624 mi/kWh [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 197]. JoyRide's Windrose sleeper, utilizing a 705 kWh Lithium-Iron Phosphate battery pack to haul general freight across Western interstate corridors at gross combination weights up to 81,600 lbs, registered a single-charge PMR of 350 to 400 miles at an average efficiency of 0.55 mi/kWh [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 170, 172].

Most notably, the 2025 measurements proved that daily productivity for long-haul BEVs is no longer strictly bound by single-charge limits, as strategic mid-route DC fast charging enabled extreme daily ranges. Saia’s linehaul Tesla Semi achieved an average of 372 miles per active day and a maximum single-day distance of 660 miles on flat-to-rolling terrain [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 197]. JoyRide's Windrose sleeper pushed the boundaries further, averaging 409 miles per active day and establishing a validated single-day maximum of 875 miles on highway-dominant corridors [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 170, 172]. These high-productivity days required precise alignment with en-route high-power charging during driver rest breaks and facility dwell times, shifting the range planning paradigm from simple battery capacity limits to integrated corridor charging logistics [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 206].

q: NACFE's 2023 white paper laid out a suggested sequence for fleets choosing a powertrain (start with BEV, then hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas/hybrids/renewable fuels, then efficient diesel as a fallback), while also acknowledging this was 'an oversimplification.' Did the real-world results of the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle, which tested all four options side by side, support a single best powertrain choice or confirm the need for fleet-specific evaluation?
expected: The 2023 white paper's 'Framework for Powertrain Decision Making' (Figure 15) suggests fleets start with BEV, fall back to hydrogen fuel cell, then natural gas/hybrids/renewable fuels, and finally efficient diesel, while explicitly noting fleets will likely need multiple, duty-cycle-specific decisions rather than one universal answer. NACFE reused this same framework graphic in the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle report, and that Run's real-world findings confirmed the 2023 premise rather than crowning one winner: 'the real-world results are that all four technologies are performing well in this segment of the market and there is no one right choice for all fleets. Rather powertrain choice depends on the intricacies of each fleet's operation, the length of haul, access to fueling/charging and a host of other factors.'
expected_loc: p.9, p.38 (2023 framework); current: run-on-less-messy-middle-blueprint-2025, p.24 (Figure 3, reused framework), p.62-63 (findings)

selected.why: The Run on Less - Messy Middle blueprint report covers the 2025 demonstration of all four powertrains side-by-side and directly addresses whether the results support a single best powertrain or fleet-specific evaluation.

This deep operational companion report provides the comprehensive cross-fleet telematics and analysis from the September 2025 Run on Less - Messy Middle, evaluating how different powertrains perform across various duty cycles.

answer:
The real-world results of the 2025 Run on Less – Messy Middle demonstration did not support a single best powertrain choice. Instead, they confirmed the critical need for fleet-specific and route-specific evaluation [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 62; Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 232]. NACFE concluded that no single technology is capable of addressing every freight application with optimal economics, environmental performance, and operational simplicity [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 228]. 

Instead, the demonstration showed that all four tested technologies—diesel, natural gas, battery electric, and hydrogen fuel cell—perform well, but each has a specific operational envelope where it excels, as well as clear physical or infrastructural boundaries where it struggles [How NACFE Helped Bring Clarity to the Messy Middle, p. 62; Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 28]. For example:
* **Diesel and Renewable Diesel:** These fleets served as the ultimate benchmark for flexibility and range. Highly optimized diesel setups achieved between 9.0 and 11.8 MPG [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 29]. This performance represents nearly double the typical industry fleet average of approximately 6.0 MPG [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 78]. Renewable diesel offered a drop-in 50% to 80% carbon intensity reduction with zero operational changes [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 252, 254].
* **Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs):** BEVs proved commercially viable for regional and selected long-haul corridors, achieving 1.5 to 2.0 kWh/mi (overall ranges between 0.44 to 6.71 mi/kWh depending on conditions) [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 29, 205]. The largest battery packs (705 kWh) achieved impressive daily averages of approximately 409 miles per active day and a maximum single-day distance of 875 miles under favorable conditions [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 170]. However, BEVs showed extreme terrain sensitivity, with efficiency dropping by 50% to 70% on grades greater than 3%, meaning route-specific terrain profiling is absolutely necessary [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 206, 252]. 
* **CNG/RNG:** Utilizing the 15-liter Cummins X15N engine, natural gas trucks delivered 4.5 to 6.7 mi/DGE [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 29]. They successfully handled very heavy-haul assignments, such as regional fuel tankers and triple dry-van configurations weighing 100,000 to 140,000 lbs. gross combination weight (GCW) [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 121, 147]. However, CNG efficiency severely degraded in low-speed, stop-and-go urban environments, establishing their ideal envelope as highway-dominant cruising with predictable station access [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 122, 254].
* **Hydrogen Fuel Cells (FCEVs):** FCEVs demonstrated rapid 10-to-15-minute refueling and a highly usable range of 350 to 450 miles on 68.6 kg of usable hydrogen [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 211, 212, 253]. Unfortunately, they remain severely restricted by high fuel costs ($15 to $25/kg) and extreme infrastructure scarcity (with only approximately 60 heavy-duty stations nationwide) [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 253, 255].

Ultimately, the 2025 demonstration proved that forcing a powertrain mismatch creates operational friction and suboptimal economics [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 68]. Because route terrain, daily mileage, payload limits, and local infrastructure vary so widely, fleets cannot rely on generic manufacturer specification sheets or a single fallback option [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 234, 253]. Instead, navigating the "Messy Middle" transition requires "portfolio thinking," where fleets actively manage mixed-technology fleets and conduct rigorous, route-specific validations to match each vehicle to its optimal application [Terrain, Technology, and Telematics: The Messy Middle Operations Report, p. 232, 233].

q: How many Guidance Reports had NACFE published on electric/hydrogen trucks as of early 2019, and how many had it published by mid-2025?
expected: As of early 2019, NACFE had produced three Guidance Reports: Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense (May 2018), Medium-Duty Electric Trucks – Cost of Ownership (October 2018), and Amping Up – Charging Infrastructure for Electric Trucks (March 2019). By mid-2025, per the Run on Less – Messy Middle report, that had grown to 11 Guidance Reports on electric and hydrogen fuel cell trucks — nearly a fourfold increase over roughly six years.

answer:
As of early 2019, NACFE had published **three** Guidance Reports focused on electric trucks [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 11]. The provided sources do not state how many Guidance Reports NACFE had published by mid-2025 because the latest provided source was published in 2023 [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 2, 3]. Because this source predates 2026 by approximately three years, its findings do not reflect publications or current technology from mid-2025. 

The three early Guidance Reports published by early 2019 are [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 11]:
1. *Electric Trucks: Where They Make Sense* (May 2018)
2. *Medium-Duty Electric Trucks – Cost of Ownership* (October 2018)
3. *Amping Up – Charging Infrastructure for Electric Trucks* (March 2019)

The closest available information from the 2023 report indicates that NACFE subsequently published "many Guidance Reports regarding the applicability of BEVs in trucking" [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 25]. Specific publications mentioned after the early 2019 period include *Viable Class 7/8 Electric, Hybrid and Alternative Fuel Tractors* (December 2019) [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 11], and the Guidance Report *Making Sense of Heavy-Duty Hydrogen Fuel Cell Tractors* (December 2020) [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 26, 41]. The 2023 report also notes plans to publish an additional "Hydrogen Guidance Report" later in 2023 [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 26-27] alongside various "Run on Less – Electric" reports detailing real-world fleet use cases [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 11].

answer:
As of December 2022, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) reported only 60 public hydrogen fueling stations in North America for all vehicle types [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 24]. Out of those 60 stations, only 4 were heavy-duty truck hydrogen fueling sites [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 24]. 

The vast majority of these public stations were highly regionalized, with 53 of the 60 stations located in California [The Messy Middle: A Time for Action, p. 24]. Because the source report was published in 2023, these figures from late 2022 may not fully reflect the current state of hydrogen refueling infrastructure.
